The wrong pair is (3) 'The Indian War of Independence 1857' - Marxist History.

According to the chapter this book was written by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and belongs to nationalistic historiography, not to Marxist history. The chapter says that the nationalistic historiography helped in the triggering of the independence movement of the Indian people against the British, and that in this aspect Savarkar's book is of great importance. Marxist history is a separate school of the post-independence era, whose Indian writers named in the chapter are Damodar Dharmanand Kosambi, Comrade Shripad Amrut Dange, Ram Sharan Sharma and Comrade Sharad Patil.

The correct pairing is: 'The Indian War of Independence, 1857' - Nationalistic historiography.

The other three pairs are correct. 'Who were the Shudras' is one of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar's books cited as an example of history of the subaltern type. 'Stripurush Tulana' was written by Tarabai Shinde and is acknowledged as the first feminist book in India. Grant Duff was a British officer who wrote 'A History of the Mahrattas', and his writing shows the British inclination of condemning Indian culture and history, so he belongs to colonial historiography.

The writing of regional history received a momentum because of the nationalistic historiography. The historians of this school wanted to restore the pride in the ancient glory of India and the self-esteem of the Indian readers, and they tried to seek the golden era of Indian history. In Maharashtra this writing was inspired by Vishnushastri Chiplunkar, who criticised the prejudiced history of ancient India written by British officers, and Vishwanath Kashinath Rajwade held the firm opinion that we should write our own history. Because of this urge to write India's own past, the attention of historians was drawn to the geographic conditions and the history of the south Indian regions as well. The same urge is seen in the writing on the Maratha period: Nilkanth Janardan Kirtane and Vishwanath Kashinath Rajwade took upon themselves the task of exposing the limitations of Grant Duff's writings, Mahadev Govind Ranade explained the background of the rise of the Maratha empire in 'The Rise of Maratha Power', and Govind Sakharam Sardesai published several volumes of Maratha history in 'Marathi Riyasat'.

Bakhar is an important type of historical document of medieval times. It contains eulogies of the heroes and stories of historic events, battles and the lives of great men, so it preserves information about the period that would otherwise be lost. Marathi bakhars are of various types, such as biographies of kings, dynastic history, descriptions of events, history of a sect, autobiographies, bakhars regarding grievance, bakhars based on mythologies, and accounts of state administration by a king. Particular bakhars are the source for particular subjects: 'Sabhasad Bakhar', written by Krishnaji Anant Sabhasad during the reign of Chhatrapati Rajaram Maharaj, is an important bakhar for getting information about the rule of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj; 'Bhausahebanchi Bakhar' describes the Battle of Panipat and 'Panipatachi Bakhar' is about the same event; and 'Holkaranchi Kaiphiyat' provides information about the Holkars and their contributions to the Maratha rule. Because of this range of subjects and this detail, bakhars are treated as an important class of historical documents.

Marxist history is one of the three ideological schools that mainly influenced Indian historiography in the post-independence era, the other two being subaltern history and feminist history. In the writings of Marxist historians the concern for the means of production, the modes of production and the industrial relations was at the centre. Accordingly, to analyse the impact of every social event of significance has remained the basic theme of Marxist historiography. In India, Marxist historians studied the transitions within the caste system. Among the notable Indian historians who adopted the Marxist ideological framework, scholars like Damodar Dharmanand Kosambi, Comrade Shripad Amrut Dange, Ram Sharan Sharma and Comrade Sharad Patil have contributed notably. Comrade Dange was one of the founder members of the Indian Communist Party, and his book 'Primitive Communism to Slavery' represents Marxist historiography. The influence of this school reached beyond itself, because the seeds of subaltern history are found in Marxist historiography. In this way Marxist history moved the focus of historical writing away from rulers and dynasties and towards the economic base of society and the social change that follows from it.

Itihasacharya Vishwanath Kashinath Rajwade was one of the two Indian historians, the other being Nilkanth Janardan Kirtane, who took upon themselves the task of exposing the limitations of Grant Duff's writings. He was of the firm opinion that we should write our own history. He is well known for his writings in Marathi on varied subjects like history, linguistics, etymology and grammar. His major contribution is that he compiled and edited 22 volumes of 'Marathyanchya Itihasachi Sadhane', and he wrote very scholarly prefaces to each of these 22 volumes. He also widened the meaning of history itself, stating, 'History is the all-inclusive image of the past societies. It does not include only the stories of political images, conspiracies and wars for seizing power.' According to him human history is defined by Time and Space, and only if a balanced combination of the three factors of Time, Space and Personalities is present does an event qualify to be called so. On method he was equally firm, insisting that history should be written only by using authentic documentary sources. To facilitate historical research he founded the 'Bharat Itihas Samshodhak Mandal' in Pune on 7th July 1910.

| Historian | Book |
|---|---|
| James Mill | 'The History of British India' |
| James Grant Duff | 'A History of the Mahrattas' |
| Mountstuart Elphinstone | 'The History of India' |
| S.A. Dange | 'Primitive Communism to Slavery' |
| Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar | 'Who were the Shudras' |

The four blanks are filled from the chapter as follows. James Grant Duff wrote 'A History of the Mahrattas', a book published in three volumes, on Maratha history. 'The History of India' was written by Mountstuart Elphinstone, Governor of Bombay (now Mumbai), and was published in 1841. S.A. Dange is Comrade Shripad Amrut Dange, one of the founder members of the Indian Communist Party, whose book 'Primitive Communism to Slavery' represents Marxist historiography. 'Who were the Shudras' is one of the two books of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar, the other being 'The Untouchables', that may be cited as examples of history of the subaltern type.

The concept map is a set of nested diamonds divided into four quadrants. In each quadrant the outermost ring names the subject that a work deals with, the middle ring names its author and the innermost ring names the work itself. One cell in each quadrant is left blank with a dotted line, so there are four blanks in all. Completed, the four sets are:

| Subject (outer ring) | Author (middle ring) | Work (inner ring) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose of Historiography | Ziauddin Barani | 'Tarikh-i-Phiruz Shahi' |
| Descriptions of the battles fought by Babur | Babur | 'Tuzuk-i-Babari' |
| The reign of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj | Krishnaji Anant Sabhasad | 'Sabhasad Bakhar' |
| History of Kashmir | Kalhana | 'Rajtarangini' |

The four cells to be filled in are therefore 'Tarikh-i-Phiruz Shahi', Babur, Krishnaji Anant Sabhasad and 'Rajtarangini'. Each is supported by the chapter. Ziauddin Barani stated the purpose of historiography in his book 'Tarikh-i-Phiruz Shahi', saying that a historian should write not only about a ruler's valour and welfare policies but also about his failings and incorrect policies. Babur, the founder of the Mughal empire, wrote the autobiography 'Tuzuk-i-Babari', which contains the descriptions of the battles fought by him. 'Sabhasad Bakhar' was written by Krishnaji Anant Sabhasad during the reign of Chhatrapati Rajaram Maharaj, and it is an important bakhar for getting information about the rule of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj. 'Rajtarangini', the history of Kashmir, was written by Kalhana in the 12th century C.E. All four works belong to the chapter's account of historiography in the medieval period.

Many European scholars felt curious about the civilisations and countries of the East, and some of them felt admiration and respect for them. These scholars were known as 'Orientalists'. They studied the similarities between Sanskrit and some of the European languages and focused more on the Vedic tradition and Sanskrit literature, and their studies resulted in formulating the notion of an ancient language that could be the mother of all Indo-European languages. In 1784 Sir William Jones founded the Asiatic Society in Kolkata, which opened the doors for research in ancient Indian literature and history. Among the Orientalist scholars Friedrich Max Muller deserves a special mention: in his opinion Sanskrit was the most ancient of the Indo-European languages, he first translated the Sanskrit text of 'Hitopadesh' into German, he was the editor of 50 volumes of 'The Sacred Books of the East', and he compiled the 'Rigveda', which has been published in six volumes, and translated it into German. Lately Edward Said, a scholar who has re-evaluated the orientalist writings, has thrown light on the imperialistic interests of the orientalist scholars.

The writings of Indian historians who were trained in the British educational system show an inclination to restore the pride in the ancient glory of India and the self-esteem of the Indian readers, and such writings are known as nationalistic historiography. Nationalistic writings in Maharashtra were inspired by Vishnushastri Chiplunkar, who criticised the prejudiced history of ancient India written by British officers. These historians tried to seek the golden era of Indian history, and they are at times blamed for ignoring the critical analysis of the historical truth. Mahadev Govind Ranade, Ramkrishna Gopal Bhandarkar, Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, Rajendra Lal Mishra, Ramesh Chandra Majumdar, Kashi Prasad Jayswal, Radha Kumud Mukherjee, Bhagawan Lal Indraji, Vasudev Vishnu Mirashi and Anant Sadashiv Altekar are some of the renowned scholars among the nationalistic historians. This historiography helped in the triggering of the independence movement of the Indian people against the British, and in this aspect Savarkar's book 'The Indian War of Independence, 1857' is of great importance. It also provided a momentum to the writing of regional histories, drawing the attention of historians to the geographic conditions and history of the south Indian regions.

Subaltern means the 'bottommost ranks', and subaltern history is history written starting from the bottommost ranks of people in the society. Its seeds are found in Marxist historiography, and the role of the Italian historian Antonio Gramsci is very important in developing this idea. Folklore has been considered a very important source for writing subaltern histories. Ranjit Guha, an Indian historian, played a major role in establishing subaltern history as an important academic school of historiography. Much before the onset of subaltern ideology, however, similar thoughts were expressed by Mahatma Jyotirao Phule and Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar. Mahatma Phule unfolded the history of the 'shudratishudra' communities in his book 'Gulamgiri' and drew attention to the exploitation of women, shudras and atishudras done under the name of religion, the terms 'shudra' and 'atishudra' indicating the bottommost ranks in the caste system. The role of the people belonging to the Dalit castes was not duly acknowledged in the colonial and nationalistic historiography, and Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar consistently wrote focusing on this fact; two of his books, 'Who Were the Shudras' and 'The Untouchables', may be cited as examples of history of the subaltern type.
